title: Compression Tap Leaks: Washer vs. Seat
description: An educational breakdown explaining why traditional compression taps drip from the spout and how degraded washers or pitted valve seats cause persistent leaks.
image_prompt: A professional 3D technical cutaway illustration of a standard brass compression tap assembly, rendered in high detail. Vertical 9:16 composition. The exterior chrome body is cut away to reveal the internal brass spindle, operating threads, black rubber seating washer, and the lower brass valve seat inside the tap chamber. Focus is centered on the junction where the rubber washer meets the valve seat. Crisp studio lighting highlights realistic metal textures, rubber grain, and clean water droplets passing through a worn edge of the washer. Clean, neutral gray background with ample soft visual space at the top and bottom third for graphic overlays. No text, no labels, no arrows, no logos, no watermarks, no fake brand names.
visual_story: The visual provides a vertical cutaway view of a compression tap interior. Viewers can see how the threaded stem drives the rubber washer down against the stationary brass seat. The visual shows a worn, uneven washer edge allowing water to bypass the seal, demonstrating that mechanical wear at this exact contact point is the primary cause of spout drips.

on_image_text.hook: Drip From The Spout? Tightening Won't Fix It.
on_image_text.explanation: Compression taps seal by forcing a rubber washer down onto a fixed internal brass seat.
on_image_text.takeaway: Replace the washer, but always check the brass seat for corrosion before reassembly.
